newsitem.title: UK: UK June retail sales up 4.5%, hit by weather - BRC.
newsitem.headline: UK June retail sales up 4.5%, hit by weather - BRC.

text.p: The value of British retail sales grew by 4.5 percent in the year to June compared with a growth rate of 4.8 percent in May, the British Retail Consortium said on Tuesday.
Sales growth over the last three months averaged 4.4 percent, the BRC said, adding that underlying volume growth remained healthy. In June last year, sales rose 7.0 percent year-on-year.
Sales suffered during a month of poor weather -- the wettest June since 1860 -- but there were still signs of "windfall" cash from building society flotations being spent.

"Whilst some sectors appear to have benefited from customers spending windfall gains, the rate of overall sales growth is down on last month," said Andrew Higginson, chairman of the BRC's economic affairs committee.

Millions of building society members are enjoying windfall payments of more than 30 billion pounds in free shares this summer as a succession of mutual lenders float on the stock exchange and convert into banks.
The BRC survey said those windfall gains were filtering into "big ticket" purchases such as electrical goods, furniture and kitchen appliances.
But poor weather dominated many sectors, with sales of women's wear particularly affected. Food prices were also depressed compared with a year ago as competition remained fierce.
Andrew Sentance, chief economic adviser to the BRC, said the latest survey mainly covered the period running up to Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on July 2.
The changes to taxes and duties announced by Brown were aimed more at the corporate sector than the consumer and would have little effect on high street spending.
"However, we have yet to see the impact of the three interest rate rises announced since the election, which are only now beginning to feed through to homeowners," Sentance said.
Base rates have been ratcheted up to 6.75 percent in three, quarter-point moves since Labour took power on May 1. The latest move came only last Thursday.

"With the pound soaring to new heights, it would make sense for the Bank of England to wait and see how consumers react over the summer months before making any further interest rate moves," Sentance said.

Higginson added that there was little sign of inflation on the high street to worry the Bank. Retailers' prices were only just over one percent up on last year, he said. "We believe that there is no need for further action to dampen demand in the near-term."
